title: Leadville Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Leadville wells have a 126 ft median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $14,200-$24,600.
h1: What Leadville Well Records Show Buyers and Builders
intro_html:
Buying land in Leadville means planning around mountain bedrock, access, and the limits of the existing well records. Within 5 miles of Leadville, Colorado, DWR records list 1,349 permitted wells. Of those, 805 are recorded as constructed, 851 report a total depth, 360 report a pump yield, and 85 report a static water level.

The records point to generally productive wells, but the information is not complete for every permit. A nearby well can help set expectations, but it does not guarantee the same result on a new lot. Site geology, fractures, elevation, casing, grout, and drilling access all affect the final outcome.

sections.heading: Leadville well depth follows the mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Leadville is 126 feet. The middle half runs from 80 to 168 feet, so a driller bidding a typical site will often be working in that range rather than assuming an unusually deep hole. Still, the 90th-percentile depth is 235 feet, and the deepest record reaches 860 feet.

Depth records show 34% of wells under 100 feet and 62% between 100 and 300 feet. Only 4% fall between 300 and 600 feet, with 0% recorded at 600 feet or more. Most permits name unnamed fractured bedrock, consistent with granite and gneiss conditions. Fractured rock can produce water at one location and poor results a short distance away, so neighboring logs are useful but not conclusive.

sections.heading: Most Leadville wells make usable household flow
sections.html:
Among the 360 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 7.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute, which is a solid range for ordinary household use when the well, pump, pressure tank, and storage system are properly sized.

The records show 75% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 16% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Low-yield results are less common but still matter: 9% are in the 1-to-5-gallon-per-minute range and 1% are under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the well completion report and pump test, not just a verbal production estimate. A strong short-term yield does not by itself prove unlimited seasonal supply.

sections.heading: Leadville water levels need a site-specific check
sections.html:
The median reported static water level is 70 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 52 and 100 feet. That information helps a contractor estimate pumping equipment, but it is not the same as well depth. Water may stand at one level and still require a deeper casing, pump setting, or storage arrangement.

The decade figures show a higher median depth to water in the 2020s than in the 2010s: 74 feet below surface compared with 60 feet. That difference is worth reviewing, but only 85 records report a static water level, and measurement conditions may differ. The series is a reason to ask for the original dates, locations, and measurements rather than treating it as proof of a basin-wide decline.

sections.heading: Leadville permit history shows continuing well activity
sections.html:
Leadville’s permit record spans several decades, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. The largest recorded permit totals are 279 in the 1990s and 272 in the 2000s. The records include 111 permits from the 2010s and 87 from the 2020s, along with older permits from the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s.

Domestic or household use accounts for 79% of the listed use mix. Monitoring wells account for 11%, while stock and irrigation make up 2% and 1%. The most active drillers in these records are Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, associated with Shelton, Joe Wayne, Twin Lakes Drilling Co., associated with Schaffer, James O, and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., associated with Shelton, Steve. Permit history helps identify local experience, but confirm current licensing, insurance, and availability before hiring.

sections.heading: A typical Leadville well budget starts with the hole
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock near Leadville, the supplied cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot for drilling. At the 126-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $8,200 to $12,600. A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at $14,200 to $24,600.

That is a planning range, not a fixed bid. A difficult access route, extra casing or grout, a deeper-than-expected hole, difficult disposal, or additional electrical work can change the price. Ask the driller to separate drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching, and electrical items. On a mountain lot, confirm that the rig can reach the proposed location before relying on a per-foot estimate.

sections.heading: Leadville buyers should investigate water and site risks
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles of Leadville, the mapped environmental inventory includes 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3,981 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped features do not establish that a particular well is contaminated, but they are enough reason to review the parcel and nearby history before closing.

Have the existing water tested through an appropriate laboratory, and ask for well construction, pump, and maintenance records. Check for low yield, seasonal changes, abandoned or dry holes, and the location of septic components. A new septic system also needs suitable soils, setbacks, access, and a permitted design. Do not assume a productive neighboring well proves your lot will drill the same way, especially in fractured granite or gneiss.

sections.heading: Before building near Leadville, verify the whole water plan
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit and completion records for the parcel and nearby wells, including Leadville North. Compare reported depth, yield, static water level, aquifer description, and use. The nearby records are dominated by unnamed fractured-bedrock wells, while 38 name an alluvial aquifer and 5 name the Unconfined San Luis Valley Aquifer. No Denver Basin aquifer wells are recorded in this area.

For a buildable lot, make the water decision before finalizing house placement, driveway grades, septic design, and utility routes. Confirm the legal use allowed by the permit; an exempt household-use well is not a general irrigation or commercial supply. If the basin or proposed use requires augmentation, resolve that with the water professionals and authorities before construction. A driller, septic designer, excavator, and electrician should review access and layout together.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Leadville?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Leadville is 126 feet. The middle half runs from 80 to 168 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 235 feet. Records range much farther, with the deepest listed well at 860 feet. Most wells are in fractured mountain bedrock, so the nearby well log matters more than the median alone.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Leadville?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 7.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. About 75% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Low yields still occur: 9% are from 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 1% are under 1 gallon per minute.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Leadville?
faq.a: The drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot for Leadville’s fractured mountain bedrock. At the 126-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,200 to $12,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $14,200 to $24,600. Access and extra depth can change the bid.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Leadville?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3,981 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby mining and environmental history before relying on it for a home.

The most active drillers in the local permit records are Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, associated with Shelton, Joe Wayne; Twin Lakes Drilling Co., associated with Schaffer, James O; and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., associated with Shelton, Steve. Use those records as a starting point, then confirm current licensing, insurance, scheduling, access requirements, and the scope of the written bid.
